Scania
SKAY-nee-a
n. (the southern province, Danish Skåne, where Malmo reformed first and the first Danish liturgy was printed in 1529)
Latin Scania, Danish and Swedish Skåne, of disputed Germanic root; Danish until 1658 and Swedish since.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Scania is the province, Danish for seven centuries and Swedish since 1658, whose chief town carried the Danish Reformation before the kingdom did. Malmo, a prosperous herring and trading port facing Copenhagen across the sound, took evangelical preaching from 1527 under Claus Mortensen and Hans Olufsen Spandemager; the town council backed them, the Grey Friars' church was given over, and in 1529 Malmo printed the first Danish evangelical service book and hymnal, the Malmo Mass, which put the liturgy, the Lord's Prayer and the congregational hymns into Danish for the first time and became the basis of the Danish rite. Frands Vormordsen, a Dutch Carmelite turned Lutheran who taught Hebrew, worked there on the Psalms and became the first evangelical superintendent of Lund. Lund itself, the ancient archbishopric of the whole north, lost its primacy at the Reformation and became a Lutheran see, and its university came only in 1666 after the Swedish conquest. The dictionary enters Scania because the first Danish liturgy and hymnal were produced by a town council and two preachers in a herring port, seven years before the kingdom was reformed by law.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a liturgy as a formulary of public prayers; a hymnal as a collection of hymns; a see as the seat of a bishop; and a primacy as the chief ecclesiastical dignity.

expand to see more

LITURGY, n. In a general sense, all public ceremonies that belong to divine service; a formulary of public prayers.

HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God; a sacred lyric sung in public worship.

SEE, n. The seat of episcopal power; a diocese; the jurisdiction of a bishop.

PRIMACY, n. The chief ecclesiastical station or dignity; the office or dignity of an archbishop.

VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.

Key Scripture

1Co 14:16 — "Else when thou shalt bless with the spirit, how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?"

Col 3:16 — "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord."

Eph 5:19 — "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;"

Psa 149:1 — "Praise ye the LORD. Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise in the congregation of saints."

Modern Corruption

Southern province, Danish until 1658, where Malmo reformed from 1527 and printed the first Danish evangelical service book and hymnal in 1529.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the congregation reduced to an audience, which a Latin liturgy enforces whether anyone intends it or not. In the old rite the people could not say the responses, could not pray the prayers and did not sing; the Malmo book of 1529 handed them all three in Danish. The apostle's objection to prayer in an unknown tongue is exactly this: “how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?” (1Co 14:16).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is congregational singing as a means of teaching, which the Reformation's hymnals were built for. The command is to teach one another, “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16), and the manner is given as “singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19). A trading town with a press obeyed the psalm's charge to “Sing unto the LORD a new song” (Psa 149:1) by printing one that herring-fishers could read.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek idiotes (G2399), the unlearned; Greek psallo (G5567), to make melody; Hebrew shir (H7892), a song.

expand to see more

Greek idiotes (G2399) — an unlearned or private person; “he that occupieth the room of the unlearned”, 1 Corinthians 14:16.

Greek eucharistia (G2169) — thanksgiving, the giving of thanks; “say Amen at thy giving of thanks”, 1 Corinthians 14:16.

Greek psalmos (G5568) — a psalm, a sacred song; “in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs”, Colossians 3:16.

Greek psallo (G5567) — to pluck, to sing, to make melody; “making melody in your heart to the Lord”, Ephesians 5:19.

Hebrew shir (H7892) — a song, a singing; “Sing unto the LORD a new song”, Psalm 149:1.

Usage

"“he that occupieth the room of the unlearned” (1Co 14:16) — a Latin rite in a Danish herring port."

"“in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16) — the Malmo hymnal of 1529."

"“Sing unto the LORD a new song” (Psa 149:1) — the first Danish evangelical service book, printed by a town council."
